query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At fusion‐relevant high temperatures, the high-temperature plastic strain and toughness of refractory high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by the mobility of edge dislocations interacting with solute-induced lattice distortions. In these alloys, enhanced lattice distortions pin the edge dislocations, raising their activation energy for glide, thereby controlling plastic flow and retarding crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a BCC HEA such as NbTaTiV or a tungsten-based HEA) with a homogeneous microstructure and typical solute distribution.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy chemistry to vary the degree of lattice distortion (for example by adding alloying elements with significantly different atomic sizes) or use controlled thermal/irradiation treatments to modify the local solute arrangements. This manipulation should selectively influence edge dislocation mobility.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical loading in the range of approximately 600–900°C, under conditions relevant to fusion plasma-facing component operation.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of edge dislocations and their interaction with local lattice distortions (from solute atoms), which dictate the onset of plastic deformation and influence crack-tip shielding.
generation.mechanism: In a highly distorted lattice, edge dislocations adopt a wavy configuration to minimize energy by sampling low-energy regions. Their mobility is then largely determined by the local solute field; at elevated temperatures, although thermal activation assists in overcoming pinning, the persistent lattice distortion limits dislocation motion. This controlled dislocation activity delays dynamic recrystallization and crack propagation, thus enhancing overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples with increased solute-induced lattice distortion will exhibit higher yield strength, more controlled (i.e., slower and more homogeneous) plastic flow, and improved toughness compared to a baseline alloy with lower lattice distortion. Specifically, in situ observations should show a higher prevalence of edge dislocation activity correlating with enhanced plastic strain resistance and delayed crack growth.
generation.baseline: A nominally similar refractory HEA with minimal additional lattice distortion (or a conventional BCC alloy where screw dislocation motion predominates) that exhibits lower high-temperature strength and toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to control plastic strain and toughness in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys under high-temperature conditions (approximately 600–900°C) typical of fusion plasma-facing components, and may not apply to multiphase alloys or systems dominated by other dislocation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: While recent evidence points to a dominant role of edge dislocations in refractory HEAs at high temperatures, the quantitative link between the extent of solute-induced lattice distortion, edge dislocation mobility, and the observed toughness remains to be precisely established. The exact threshold of lattice distortion necessary to achieve the desired mechanical behavior is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA specimens: one set with an intentionally increased level of solute-induced lattice distortion (via alloying with atoms that have large size mismatches) and a control set with minimal lattice distortion. Conduct high-temperature tensile tests (600–900°C) while performing in situ TEM or neutron diffraction to monitor dislocation character and density. Compare mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, fracture toughness) and correlate them with the observed edge dislocation activity.
measurements: Yield strength and tensile ductility from high-temperature tensile tests
Dislocation type and density (especially edge vs. screw) using in situ TEM or neutron diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy samples with enhanced lattice distortions do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength, controlled (i.e., more homogeneous and slower) plastic deformation mediated by edge dislocations, and improved toughness relative to the control specimens, then the hypothesis that edge dislocation–solute interactions govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in these materials is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The excellent plasticity of the present refractory HEA can be predicted by the relationship between the polycrystalline elastic moduli, such as the Cauchy pressure (C12 − C44) (), Pugh ratio [bulk modulus (K)/shear modulus (G)] (), and Poisson’s ratio (ν) (). Moreover, we investigated the type of mobile dislocations using the neutron diffraction (ND) peak-broadening modeling and analysis using the Williamson-Hall plot method (), experimentally verified by the high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) technique. It is found that the dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals. These new discoveries of unique elastic and plastic deformation behaviors in the NbTaTiV refractory HEA will facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaTiV alloy is predicted to be intrinsically ductile, based on the ductility criteria, using the Cauchy pressure, Pugh ratio, and Poisson’s ratio. The verification of the mobile dislocation type was quantitatively investigated using the Williamson-Hall plot profile, experimentally verified by the HAADF-STEM. The dominant mobile dislocation is determined to be the character of edge dislocations during the 15% plastic deformation at elevated temperatures. It is thought that the severely distorted lattice induces the deviation of the formation of dislocations from their neutral dislocation planes, which, consequently, leads to a substantial reduction in the mobility of edge dislocations during plastic deformation. Thus, the edge dislocations are believed to be the dominant dislocation type for the BCC refractory HEA, which is atypical, as compared to the conventional BCC metals and alloys. cited_evidence.text: To further cement that the edge dislocations can control the strength, we apply a new theory for the yield strength versus temperature and strain rate for edge dislocations moving through a random BCC alloy. In the theory, each alloying element is viewed as a solute that interacts with a dislocation in a hypothetical homogeneous “average” alloy that has all the macroscopic properties of the true random alloy. Fluctuations in the local arrangements of solutes create large local variations in the potential energy for the dislocation. The dislocation thus spontaneously adopts a low-energy wavy structure to take advantage of the low-energy solute environments and avoid the high-energy environments.
